meaning: The case particle 「を」: placed after a noun it marks the direct object of a transitive verb (including 「〜をする」); before a verb of movement it marks the place passed through or the point of departure.
connection: Noun + を + transitive verb; place noun + を + verb of movement (歩く, 渡る, 出る, 降りる, etc.)

senses.label: Object of an action
senses.meaning: Marks the person or thing directly affected by the action, like the object after an English verb. But Japanese word order is “object + を + verb”: the verb comes last. 「を」 is pronounced “o”.
senses.connection: Noun + を + 食べる／飲む／見る／読む／書く／買う and other transitive verbs
examples: I eat bread every morning.
Yesterday I bought a magazine at the bookstore.
I watch TV every evening.

senses.label: 「〜をする」
senses.meaning: An activity noun before 「する」 is marked with 「を」. It means “do (an activity)”. You can use it for sports, study, work, housework and more.
senses.connection: Noun + を + する (テニスをする／宿題をする／料理をする)
examples: On weekends I play tennis with friends.
Did you do your homework?
On Sunday I cleaned my room.

senses.label: Place passed through
senses.meaning: Shows that you move through, across or along a place: “walk along”, “go through”, “cross”. Common verbs are 「歩く」, 「走る」, 「渡る」, 「通る」, 「散歩する」, 「曲がる」 and 「飛ぶ」.
senses.connection: Place + を + 歩く／走る／渡る／通る／散歩する／曲がる／飛ぶ
examples: I take a walk in the park every morning.
Please cross this bridge.
Turn right at the next corner.

senses.label: Starting point you leave
senses.meaning: Shows the place you leave or get out of: “leave”, “get out of”, “get off”. Common verbs are 「出る」, 「降りる」, 「出発する」 and 「卒業する」.
senses.connection: Place + を + 出る／降りる／出発する／卒業する／離れる
examples: I leave home at seven every morning.
I get off the train at the next station.
My older brother graduated from university last year.

notes: The objects of 「好き」, 「わかる」, 「できる」, 「ほしい」 and 「上手」 take 「が」, not 「を」: ✕「日本語をわかります」→ ○「日本語がわかります」.
The person you meet with 「会う」 and the vehicle you get on with 「乗る」 take 「に」, not 「を」: ✕「友達を会う」→ ○「友達に会う」; ✕「電車を乗る」→ ○「電車に乗る」.
「大学を出る」 usually means “to graduate from university”; to say “walk out of the campus” you use 「大学から出る」. Changing the particle changes the meaning.
Getting on takes 「に」 and getting off takes 「を」. Mix them up and the sentence is wrong: ✕「電車を乗る」→ ○「電車に乗る」; ✕「電車に降りる」→ ○「電車を降りる」.
「歩く」 and 「出る」 are intransitive verbs, but they still take 「を」 for the route or the place you leave. Don't switch to 「が」 just because the verb is intransitive: ✕「公園が散歩する」→ ○「公園を散歩する」.

daily.description: Telling the staff what you'd like to eat.
daily.example: I'll have ramen.

etymology: One theory says 「を」 was originally an interjection-like particle used for emotion or emphasis, and later became fixed as the case particle for objects. It was pronounced “wo” in old Japanese and “o” today. Under modern kana rules, only this particle keeps the spelling 「を」. The uses marking the place passed through and the point of departure already existed in Old Japanese and have survived into the modern language.
formation: 「を」 is a single case particle that marks the preceding noun as “what the action covers or affects”, in the pattern noun + を + verb, with the verb at the end. Because the relations are fixed by the particle rather than word order, moving the object before the subject does not change the meaning. After a transitive verb, what is “affected” is the person or thing directly acted on, the object (「パンを食べる」), and 「〜をする」 likewise treats an activity noun as the object of 「する」. After a verb of movement, what is “covered” is a stretch of space: 「道を歩く」 takes the whole road as the route traveled, and 「家を出る」 takes the house as the point left behind, which is why 「歩く」 and 「出る」 take 「を」 even though they are intransitive. Unlike 「で」, which only says where an action takes place, 「を」 makes the place part of the movement itself; that is the difference between 「道を歩く」 (walk along the road) and 「道で遊ぶ」 (play on the road).

similar.title: 〜をください
similar.explanation: A set phrase built on this use (same origin): 「を」 marks the thing you want, and 「ください」 turns it into a request. Used when shopping or ordering: 「水をください」.

similar.title: 〜が好き・〜が嫌い・〜が上手・〜が下手
similar.explanation: In English “like” and “be good at” take a direct object, so learners often compare them with 「を」. But 「好き」 and 「上手」 are adjectives, so the thing liked takes 「が」: 「音楽が好きです」, not 「音楽を好きです」 (heard occasionally in speech, but not standard).

similar.title: 〜がわかる・〜ができる
similar.explanation: In English you “understand Japanese” or “can swim” with a direct object, but 「わかる」 and 「できる」 express ability or a state, so their object takes 「が」: 「日本語がわかります」, 「テニスができます」. This contrasts neatly with the rule “the object of an action takes を”.

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when talking about leaving. 「から」 highlights the starting point, “out from inside”, and works with any action (in 「家から駅まで歩く」 you can't use 「を」). 「を」 only goes with leaving verbs like 「出る」, 「降りる」 or 「離れる」 and expresses leaving in general. Both 「部屋から出る」 and 「部屋を出る」 are fine, but 「大学を出る」 usually means graduating.

meaning: The basic meaning of the particle 「に」 is “the point where an action lands”: it marks the destination of movement, the place you go into, the person an action is aimed at, a point in time, the place where something exists, and also “A with B” / “A plus B” combinations.
connection: Place / person / time / location of existence + に + verb; noun A + に + noun B
etymology: 「に」 is an ancient case particle whose basic function is to mark the “point” where an action is located or lands. The arrival point in space, a point in time, the place where something exists and the person an action is aimed at are all the same kind of “point”; the idea of “attaching to something” further extends to the additive sense “A plus B”. One theory holds that the copula 「なり」 developed from 「に＋あり」.
formation: The basic meaning of 「に」 is “the point where an action finally arrives or lands”, and each sense is just that point landing somewhere different. In space it is the destination or the place you enter or board (「駅に着く」, 「バスに乗る」); on a person it is the target an action or object finally reaches (「友達に手紙を書く」); on the timeline it is a clock time or date (「六時に起きる」); in a state it is the place where something exists or lives (「東京に住む」); and “attaching to something” extends to the combination “A plus B” (「ご飯にみそ汁」). Once you grasp this core idea of a “point”, it is clear why 「に」 can follow places, people, times and things.

senses.label: Destination
senses.meaning: Marks where you are going or arriving: “go to”, “come to”, “return to”, “arrive at”. Often used with 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」 and 「着く」.
senses.connection: Place + に + 行く／来る／帰る／着く
examples: I'm going to the bank tomorrow.
I go home at six every day.
The plane arrived at the airport at ten.

senses.label: Place you enter or get on
senses.meaning: Marks the place you go into, get on or go up into: “enter”, “get on”. Often used with 「入る」, 「乗る」 and 「上がる」.
senses.connection: Place／vehicle + に + 入る／乗る／上がる
examples: I take a bath every evening.
I got on the bus at the station.
Please come into the room.

senses.label: Person the action is aimed at
senses.meaning: Marks the person an action is directed at: “to”, “for”, “with”. Often used with 「あげる」, 「電話する」, 「会う」, 「聞く」, 「教える」 and 「手紙を書く」.
senses.connection: Person + に + あげる／電話する／会う／聞く／教える／書く
examples: I gave a present to my friend.
Yesterday I called my mother.
I ran into my teacher at the station.

senses.label: Clock time, date, day of the week
senses.meaning: Shows the specific point in time when something happens. Times, dates and years with numbers, and days of the week, usually take 「に」. Like “at six”, “on the 5th”, “in 2020”.
senses.connection: Number + 時／分／日／月／年 + に; 〜曜日 + に
examples: I get up at six every morning.
On Sunday I went to see a movie.
I came to Japan in 2020.

senses.label: Where someone or something is
senses.meaning: Shows that a person or thing exists somewhere. The common pattern is 「place に + thing が + ある」 or 「place に + person が + いる」, like “There is ... in/on ...”. Use 「ある」 for non-living things and 「いる」 for people and animals.
senses.connection: Place + に + noun + が + あります／います
examples: There is a book on the desk.
There is a cat in the yard.
There is a big supermarket near the station.

senses.label: Living and staying
senses.meaning: With verbs like 「住む」, 「泊まる」, 「勤める」 and 「座る」, it shows where you stay, for a long time or a short time: “live in”, “stay at”, “sit on”.
senses.connection: Place + に + 住む／泊まる／勤める／座る／置く
examples: I live in Tokyo.
Tonight I'm staying at a hotel.
Please have a seat in this chair.

senses.label: Classic combination
senses.meaning: Two things that commonly go together, like “A with B”. Many proverbs use this form.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun (ご飯にみそ汁, 梅に鶯, 鬼に金棒)
examples: The classic Japanese breakfast is rice with miso soup.
That team with that coach — it's like giving a demon an iron club. They're unstoppable.

senses.label: Plus, and
senses.meaning: When ordering or listing, it means “A, plus B”. Casual and common in speech.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun + を / が (コーヒーにケーキを)
examples: A coffee and a slice of cake, please.
For dinner I made curry and a salad.

notes: With giving and receiving verbs, the direction of 「に」 can flip: 「友達に本をあげる」 means giving a book to a friend; 「友達に本をもらう」 means getting a book from a friend. Look at the verb to work out the direction; get it wrong and the meaning is reversed.
Getting on takes 「に」 and getting off takes 「を」: ✕「バスを乗る」→ ○「バスに乗る」; ✕「バスに降りる」→ ○「バスを降りる」.
Relative time words such as 「今日」, 「明日」, 「昨日」, 「毎日」, 「今」, 「来週」 and 「去年」 don't take 「に」: ✕「明日に行きます」→ ○「明日行きます」.
The place where an action happens takes 「で」, not 「に」: ✕「図書館に勉強します」→ ○「図書館で勉強します」. Use 「に」 only for existing or staying somewhere.
When a verb follows, 「に」 is easily read as the target of the action: 「母に花を買った」 means “I bought flowers for my mother”, not “I bought my mother and flowers”. For ordinary “A and B” lists, use 「と」.

similar.title: 〜へ (direction)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when marking a destination, and mostly interchangeable: 「学校に行く」, 「学校へ行く」. 「に」 focuses on the point of arrival and can also mark the person an action is directed at; 「へ」 focuses on the direction of movement.

similar.title: 〜に行く・〜に来る (purpose)
similar.explanation: The same 「に」 (same origin), both pointing to “where you're heading”. In 「図書館に行く」, 「に」 follows a place and marks the destination; in 「本を借りに行く」, 「に」 follows a verb's ます-stem and marks the purpose of going.

similar.title: 〜までに
similar.explanation: Both involve a point in time and are often compared: 「五時に帰る」 means going home at five o'clock; 「五時までに帰る」 means going home any time before five (a deadline).

similar.title: 〜がある・〜がいる (existence)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and often used together. This entry focuses on the place of existence marked by 「に」; 「がある／がいる」 focuses on what exists and on the difference between 「ある」 (things) and 「いる」 (people and animals).

similar.title: 〜に加えて
similar.explanation: Both rest on the “addition” sense of 「に」. 「〜に加えて」 is the written “in addition to …” and is followed by a full sentence; 「AにB」 simply pairs two nouns in a short way.

meaning: The particle 「で」 marks the place where an action happens (“at / in ~”) after a place noun, and the means used (“by / with ~”) after a vehicle, tool, method or language.
connection: Place noun + で + action verb; vehicle / tool / method / language + で + 行く／書く／話す, etc.
etymology: 「で」 comes from the old case particle 「にて」 through a sound change (にて→んで→で), and spread from the end of the Heian period. 「にて」 itself marked place, means, cause and more, which is why modern 「で」 has all these uses.
formation: 「で」 is generally thought to come from classical 「にて」: 「に」 (the point where something is) + the conjunctive particle 「て」, meaning “being in a place, (do something)”. So 「で」 marks the stage or setting where an action is carried out, not the end point the action reaches. Because it means “do something in a place”, it needs an action or event as the predicate. Pure existence (「いる」, or 「ある」 for objects) has no action, so it takes 「に」 instead of 「で」. The same “setting” can also be a tool, a method or a cause, which is why 「で」 also expresses means.

senses.label: Place of an action
senses.meaning: Shows where an action takes place: “do ... at/in ...”. It comes before action verbs like 「勉強する」, 「食べる」, 「遊ぶ」, 「働く」 and 「買う」.
senses.connection: Place + で + 勉強する／食べる／遊ぶ／働く／買う／待つ
examples: I study at the library every day.
Yesterday I bought shoes at a department store.
Please wait here for a moment.

senses.label: Place of an event
senses.meaning: Shows where an activity, event or party is held, or where something happens. 「ある」 is used here, but it means “take place”, so the place takes 「で」, not 「に」.
senses.connection: Place + で + noun (パーティー／試験／事故 etc.) + が + ある
examples: There's an exam at school tomorrow.
There's a party at a friend's house on Saturday.
There was an accident in front of the station.

senses.label: Transportation
senses.meaning: Shows what you travel by: “by bus”, “by train”. It comes before movement verbs like 「行く」, 「来る」 and 「帰る」.
senses.connection: Vehicle + で + 行く／来る／帰る
examples: I go to school by bus every day.
I came to the station by bicycle.
I'm going from Tokyo to Osaka by Shinkansen.

senses.label: Tool / method
senses.meaning: Shows the tool or method you use to do something: “with”, “by”. This includes chopsticks, pens, phones, email and so on.
senses.connection: Tool・method + で + 食べる／書く／切る／連絡する
examples: Japanese people eat rice with chopsticks.
Please write your name in pen.
I'll send the details by email.

senses.label: Language
senses.meaning: Shows which language you speak or write in: “in Japanese”, “in English”.
senses.connection: 日本語／英語／中国語 etc. + で + 話す／書く／言う
examples: Let's speak in Japanese.
How do you say this in Japanese?
I wrote a letter in English.

notes: Existence takes 「に」, actions take 「で」: ✕「部屋で猫がいる」→ ○「部屋に猫がいる」; ✕「公園に遊ぶ」→ ○「公園で遊ぶ」.
「住む」 takes 「に」: ✕「大阪で住んでいます」→ ○「大阪に住んでいます」. But 「大阪で働いています」 uses 「で」.
Don't say 「足で」 for going on foot: ✕「足で行きます」→ ○「歩いて行きます」.
A vehicle with 「で」 is followed by 「行く」 or 「来る」, not 「乗る」: ✕「バスで乗ります」→ ○「バスに乗ります」 / ○「バスで行きます」.
「日本語で話す」 means “speak (about something) in Japanese”; 「日本語を話す」 means “speak Japanese (the language)”. The focus is different, so they aren't freely interchangeable.

work.example: Please wait here.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express a means or method, but 「によって」 belongs to written language and formal explanations and sounds formal: 「インターネットによって情報を集める」. In everyday speech, 「で」 is the usual choice.

similar.title: 〜ことで (means)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「で」 follows a noun (「電話で」); 「ことで」 follows a verb and turns a whole action into the means: 「毎日練習することで上手になる」.

meaning: Comes after a place or direction noun and shows the direction or destination of movement: “to”, “toward”. Pronounced “e”.
connection: Place・direction noun + へ + movement verb

senses.label: Direction of movement
senses.meaning: Shows movement toward a direction or place: “go to”, “come toward”. It comes before movement verbs like 「行く」, 「来る」, 「帰る」 and 「向かう」. As a particle, 「へ」 is pronounced “e”.
senses.connection: Place + へ + 行く／来る／帰る／向かう
examples: I'm going to Osaka next week.
Let's head home early.
This way, please.

senses.label: 「〜への」 before a noun
senses.meaning: Adding 「の」 after 「へ」 lets it describe a noun: “a letter to ...”, “the way to ...”. 「に」 can't take 「の」 directly.
senses.connection: Noun + への + noun (手紙／プレゼント／道 etc.)
examples: This is a letter to my mother.
Please tell me the way to the station.

senses.label: Addressee of a letter or message
senses.meaning: Used at the start of a letter or message, like “To ...” or “Dear ...”. Also used in the welcome phrase 「ようこそ〜へ」.
senses.connection: Name／title + へ; ようこそ + place + へ
examples: Dear Mom, thank you for everything.
Welcome to Japan!

notes: The particle 「へ」 is pronounced “e”, not “he”, and it isn't written 「え」: ✕「学校え行きます」.
When the action is directed at a person, use 「に」, not 「へ」: ✕「友達へ会います」→ ○「友達に会います」.
To modify a noun, use 「への」; 「にの」 doesn't exist: ✕「母にの手紙」→ ○「母への手紙」.
Writing 「〇〇さんへ」 on a card or note to someone you know is fine. But in business emails and formal letters, the address line is usually just 「〇〇様」 without 「へ」; adding it sounds too casual.

etymology: 「へ」 was originally the noun 「辺（へ）」, meaning “edge, side, area”. It later became a particle of direction. Its sound changed from “he” to “e” through a sound shift after the Heian period (「ハ行転呼」), but the spelling 「へ」 remains.

similar.title: 〜に (destination / target)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning when marking a destination, and mostly interchangeable: 「駅に行く」, 「駅へ行く」. 「に」 focuses on the point of arrival and can also mark the person an action is directed at; 「へ」 focuses on the direction.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: Both express where a movement goes and are often compared: 「駅へ行く」 means heading for the station; 「駅まで歩く」 stresses walking all the way to the station (the limit you reach).

similar.title: 〜への・〜での・〜からの (particle + の)
similar.explanation: Built by adding 「の」 to this use (same origin): 「へ」 can't modify a noun on its own, but with 「の」 it becomes 「への」, as in 「日本への旅行」 or 「先生への手紙」.

formation: 「へ」 was originally the noun 「辺（へ）」, meaning “the area around, the edge”. 「学校へ行く」 first meant something like “go toward the area of the school”, so 「へ」 focuses on the direction of movement rather than stressing arrival at an exact point the way 「に」 does. Because it expresses “facing toward something”, it naturally extends to “one's feelings directed toward someone”: 「母へ」 (to Mom). The pronunciation later changed from “he” to “e”, but the spelling 「へ」 was kept.

meaning: After a noun or particle it adds a like item, “also, too”; 「AもBも」 means “both A and B”. After a quantity it stresses that the amount is large (“as many as, a full”; 「何回も」 “many times”), and with a negative it means “not even one”.
connection: Noun + も (replaces は／が／を); noun + particle (に・で・と etc.) + も; quantity + も; 何 + counter + も; 一 + counter + も + negative

senses.label: Also / too
senses.meaning: Shows that something is the same as what was mentioned before: “... too”, “... also”. When you use 「も」, it replaces 「は」, 「が」 or 「を」.
senses.connection: Noun + も (replaces は／が／を); noun + に／で／と + も
examples: I'm a student too.
I'll take this one too, please.
I also went to Kyoto.

senses.label: Both A and B
senses.meaning: 「AもBも」 means both are true: “both A and B”. With a negative, it means “neither A nor B”.
senses.connection: Noun + も + noun + も
examples: Both my father and my mother are well.
I like both meat and fish.
Today both the rain and the wind are strong.

senses.label: Stressing a large amount
senses.meaning: After a number or amount, it shows the speaker feels it's a lot or a long time: “as many as”, “a whole ...”.
senses.connection: Number／amount + も
examples: I waited a whole hour at the station.
I ate three pieces of cake!
I've already read this book three times.

senses.label: 何 + counter + も
senses.meaning: 「何 + counter + も」 means many times or many people: “many”, “over and over”.
senses.connection: 何 + counter + も (「何度も」, 「何回も」, 「何人も」)
examples: I've seen that movie many times.
I called him over and over, but he didn't answer.

senses.label: Not even one
senses.meaning: 「一 + counter + も」 with a negative is a total denial: “not a single”, “not at all”.
senses.connection: 一 + counter + も + negative (「一円もない」, 「一人もいない」)
examples: I don't have a single yen in my wallet.
There wasn't a single person in the classroom.

notes: 「は」, 「が」 and 「を」 can't be stacked with 「も」; replace them with 「も」: ✕「私はも」→ ○「私も」; ✕「パンをも食べた」→ ○「パンも食べた」.
「も」 assumes that “the same thing has already been mentioned”. If you say 「私も学生です」 when introducing yourself with no such context, people will think someone else was mentioned before.
A quantity + 「も」 stresses “that many”, with surprise or annoyance: saying 「三十分も待ちました」 to someone who's late sounds like a reproach. If you don't want to blame them, say 「三十分待ちました」.
「も」 means the speaker thinks it's “a lot”, while 「しか〜ない」 means “few”; mix them up and your attitude flips: 「三人も来た」 (three people came, more than expected) ≠ 「三人しか来なかった」 (only three came).
「一」 + counter + 「も」 must be followed by a negative: ✕「一人もいた」→ ○「一人もいなかった」.

etymology: 「も」 is a binding particle that has existed since ancient times; its basic function is to mark “addition of a like item”. The paired form 「AもBも」 is just as old, and after a quantity it extended to the emphasis “as many as this”. The same 「も」 is also found in words such as 「けれども」 and 「ども」.
formation: 「も」 is a binding particle whose core idea is “adding this item to the like items already known”. So 「私も学生です」 presupposes that someone else is already a student and “I” am added to them. It occupies the same slot as 「は」, 「が」 and 「を」, so it replaces them rather than stacking. In 「AもBも」 each of the two is added in turn, giving “both A and B”. After a quantity, it “adds” on top of the amount the speaker expected, as if saying “it even reached this number”, which produces the surprise and emphasis of “as many as that”; 「何回も」 and 「何度も」 mean the count is too high to tally, i.e. “many times”. After the smallest unit such as 「一つ」 or 「一人」, or after a question word, plus a negative, the minimum (or any item at all) is added and negated one by one, giving the total negation “not even one”. So “also”, “both”, “as many as” and “not even one” all grow from the single core idea of addition.

similar.title: 〜は (topic)
similar.explanation: Both are binding particles that present the topic, and they're the pair most often compared: 「私は学生です」 is a plain statement; 「私も学生です」 means someone else is already a student and “I am too”.

similar.title: 〜question word + も〜ない (total negation)
similar.explanation: Built on this 「も」 (same origin): “question word + も + negative” is a total negation. 「何も食べない」 means “eat nothing”, not “also”.

similar.title: 〜という〜 (emphasizing numbers)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜という〜」 sits between a number and a noun and also stresses a large amount (「百万人という人が集まった」); it's more written and formal than 「も」.

meaning: 「の」 links a noun to what follows: it marks possession, attributes and apposition; it can stand in for a noun already understood ("...'s one"), replace 「が」 for the subject inside a noun-modifying clause, or turn a whole sentence into a noun after a plain-form verb.
connection: Noun + の + noun; noun / adjective + の (standing for a noun); noun + の + verb / adjective + noun (subject); plain-form verb / い-adjective, な-adjective + な + の (nominalizer)

senses.label: Ownership / belonging
senses.meaning: Shows who something belongs to: “my”, “Tanaka's”, “the company's”.
senses.connection: Person・organization + の + noun
examples: This is my book.
Mr. Tanaka's car is white.
Please tell me the company's phone number.

senses.label: Type, content, origin
senses.meaning: Shows the kind, content, origin, material or time of the second noun. English often just puts the nouns side by side, but Japanese still needs 「の」: 「日本語の先生」 (Japanese teacher), 「日本の車」 (Japanese car).
senses.connection: Noun + の + noun (origin／content／material／time etc.)
examples: The Japanese teacher is very kind.
This is a Japanese car.
Where is yesterday's newspaper?

senses.label: Apposition / position
senses.meaning: Shows that both nouns are the same person or thing (apposition), or shows a position. Like “my friend Tanaka” or “on top of the desk”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + name; noun + の + 上／中／前 etc.
examples: Let me introduce my friend Tanaka.
The key is on the desk.

senses.label: Noun + の (“...'s”)
senses.meaning: In 「noun + の」, a known noun after it is left out. 「私の」 means “mine”, 「田中さんの」 means “Tanaka's”.
senses.connection: Noun + の (+ です／は／を etc.)
examples: This umbrella is mine.
Which one is Mr. Tanaka's?
This dictionary isn't the teacher's.

senses.label: Adjective + の (“the ... one”)
senses.meaning: 「adjective + の」 means “the one with this quality”: “the red one”, “the big one”, “a cheaper one”. Common when shopping or choosing.
senses.connection: い-adjective + の; な-adjective + な + の
examples: I'll take that red one, please.
Do you have a slightly cheaper one?
A quiet one would be good.

senses.label: Subject in a clause (replacing が)
senses.meaning: 「の」 marks the subject (the doer) of the clause. 「母の作った料理」＝「母が作った料理」. It sounds a little more literary and gentle.
senses.connection: Noun + の + verb plain form + noun
examples: The food my mother makes is delicious.
This is the town where I was born.
On rainy days, I stay home.

senses.label: As subject or topic
senses.meaning: Turns “doing something” into a subject or topic, followed by an evaluating adjective. Like “-ing” or “to ...” in English.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + のは／のが + 難しい・楽しい・好きだ・上手だ, etc.
examples: Speaking Japanese is difficult.
I like cooking.
Getting up early in the morning is hard.

senses.label: What you perceive
senses.meaning: Followed by perception verbs like 「見る」, 「聞く」, 「聞こえる」, 「感じる」, it shows a scene you saw or heard directly. Here only 「の」 works, not 「こと」.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + のを + 見る／聞く; 〜のが + 見える／聞こえる
examples: I saw the children playing in the park.
I can hear someone singing in the next room.

notes: In English two nouns can simply sit side by side (“Japanese teacher”, “city map”), but in Japanese a noun modifying a noun must take 「の」: ✕「私母」→ ○「私の母」.
Verbs and adjectives modify nouns directly, without 「の」. This is a very common mistake: ✕「食べるの物」→ ○「食べる物」; ✕「大きいの家」→ ○「大きい家」. な-adjectives use 「な」: 「静かな部屋」.
Using 「の」 to refer to a person treats them like a thing and is impolite: ✕「あの背が高いのは誰ですか」→ ○「あの背が高い人は誰ですか」. For superiors or clients, use 「方」: 「あちらの方」.
「が」 can become 「の」 only inside a clause that modifies a noun. The subject of the main sentence can't be changed: ✕「母の料理を作った」 turns into “(someone) cooked Mom's dish” → ○「母が料理を作った」.
Before verbs of perception (見る・聞く・見える・聞こえる), only 「の」 works: ✕「彼が歌うことを聞いた」→ ○「彼が歌うのを聞いた」.

etymology: 「の」 is an adnominal case particle that already existed in Old Japanese, used to connect nouns. In the classical language 「が」 did the same job, and it survives today in 「我が国」 and 「我が家」. 「の」 could also mark the subject in Old Japanese, which is why it can still replace 「が」 inside noun-modifying clauses today. When the following noun is dropped, 「の」 becomes a pro-nominal particle (準体助詞), and from there it developed into a nominalizer for whole clauses.
formation: The core use is “noun A + の + noun B”: A becomes a modifier of B, meaning “the B that belongs to the range of A”; whether it reads as possession, origin, content or location is decided by the two nouns themselves. When the head noun B is dropped, 「の」 occupies the noun slot and means “the one that...” (「私のです」, 「赤いの」). If the following “verb + noun” is seen as one big noun, the preceding noun can attach to it with 「の」, so 「の」 marks the subject of the clause (「母の作った料理」). Attached after a whole sentence, 「の」 stands for “the matter / the action”, turning the sentence into a noun (「歌うのが好き」). All of these come from one core: 「の」 links and stands in for a noun, and has no concrete meaning of its own — the surrounding words fill it in.

similar.title: 〜な + noun (na-adjectives before nouns)
similar.explanation: Both are used to modify nouns and are often compared: a noun modifying a noun uses 「の」 (「日本の車」); a な-adjective modifying a noun uses 「な」 (「きれいな車」).

similar.title: 〜が (subject)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mark the subject. 「が」 works in any sentence; 「の」 can replace 「が」 only inside a clause that modifies a noun, and sounds slightly more written and softer.

similar.title: 〜こと (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both turn a sentence into a noun. 「の」 is more concrete and colloquial, and is the only option before perception verbs; 「こと」 is more abstract and formal, and is the only option in 「〜ことができる」 and 「趣味は〜ことだ」.

similar.title: 〜ということ (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both turn content into a noun. 「〜ということ」 presents information, news or a claim as content (「明日休みだということを知った」); 「の」 is mostly used for actions and events right in front of you.

similar.title: 〜のが好き・〜のが上手 (verb nominalization)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this is the most common set phrase with nominalizing 「の」, meaning “like / be good at doing something”: 「歌うのが好き」.

meaning: The particle 「か」 carries a core sense of uncertainty. At the end of a sentence it makes a question; between nouns or clauses it offers a choice; inside a sentence it forms an embedded question; and in a rhetorical tone it expresses strong denial.
connection: Question: sentence (です／ます or plain form) + か; choice: noun + か + noun; embedded question: question word … plain form + か; rhetorical: plain / volitional form + か

senses.label: Polite questions
senses.meaning: Follows 「です」 or 「ます」 to form a polite question. In writing, the sentence often ends with 「。」, though 「？」 is also fine. Say it with a rising tone.
senses.connection: 〜です／〜ます／〜ました／〜ません + か
examples: Are you a student?
Are you going to school tomorrow?
Where is the restroom?

senses.label: Casual questions
senses.meaning: Adding 「か」 to the plain form makes a casual question. It sounds direct and is mostly used by men. In everyday speech people usually skip 「か」 and just use a rising tone or 「の」: 「行く？」, 「行くの？」. Nouns and な-adjectives drop 「だ」: 「学生か？」.
senses.connection: Verb・い-adjective plain form + か; noun・な-adjective + か (drop 「だ」)
examples: Are you coming too?
Is it really that expensive?
You're going home already?

senses.label: 「そうですか」 for “I see”
senses.meaning: Said with a falling tone, 「そうですか」 or 「そうか」 isn't a question. It means “Oh, I see” or “Is that so”, accepting what the other person said.
senses.connection: そうですか／そうか (falling tone)
examples: A: Tomorrow is a day off. B: Oh, I see.
I see. Got it.

senses.label: Choosing between nouns
senses.meaning: 「AかB」 means one of A and B: “A or B”. Often used to offer a choice or to show uncertainty.
senses.connection: Noun + か + noun
examples: Water or tea, please.
I'll go by train or bus.
Please decide quickly whether you're going or not.

senses.label: As an object
senses.meaning: Uses a “who / what / where” question as the object, followed by 「分かる」, 「知る」, 「教える」, 「覚える」, and so on. The 「を」 after 「か」 is usually dropped.
senses.connection: Question word ... plain form + か + 分かる／知っている／教えてください／覚えている
examples: Please tell me where the station is.
Do you know who's coming?
I don't remember what I ate yesterday.

senses.label: As a topic or subject
senses.meaning: The question clause is followed by 「は」 or 「が」 and becomes the topic or subject. Common as 「〜かは分からない」 or 「〜かが大事だ」.
senses.connection: Question word ... plain form + か + は／が + predicate
examples: When we leave hasn't been decided yet.
How you explain it is what matters.

senses.label: As if ...!
senses.meaning: Said with falling intonation in speech to strongly deny or refuse: "No way I'd ...!" Often paired with 「誰が」 or 「そんなこと」. Rough in tone, mostly used by men.
senses.connection: Plain form + か (！) (誰が信じるか, 知るか)
examples: Who'd believe a story like that!
How should I know!
As if I'd lose to a guy like that!

senses.label: Could it possibly ...?
senses.meaning: In writing, 「〜（よ）うか」, 「〜だろうか」, 「〜であろうか」 ask rhetorically, "Could ... ever be? (Never.)" Solemn in tone; common in essays and speeches.
senses.connection: Verb volitional / conjectural form + か (あろうか, 言えようか, 〜だろうか)
examples: Could there be any greater joy than this?
Who could blame him?
Is it really all right to just leave it like this?

notes: Plain-form questions between friends usually drop 「か」 and use rising intonation: 「行く？」. 「行くか？」 sounds stiff and masculine, and can come across as rude to women or people you don't know well.
「そうですか」 with falling intonation means “I see”; with rising intonation it means “Really?” with some doubt. Change the intonation and the meaning changes.
「か」 means one of two, 「と」 means both: 「コーヒーと紅茶を買う」 is buying both; 「コーヒーか紅茶を買う」 is buying one of them.
A question embedded in a sentence must be in the plain form; you can't keep 「ですか」: ✕「駅はどこですか教えてください」→ ○「駅はどこか教えてください」 (more polite: 「駅がどこか教えていただけますか」).
Rising and falling tones mean opposite things: 「行くか？」(rising) is "Are you going?", while 「行くか！」(falling) is "Like hell I'm going!" In writing, rely on cues such as 「誰が」and 「！」.

etymology: 「か」 is an old particle. It could appear in the middle of a sentence (as a binding particle, 「係助詞」) or at the end to show a question or a rhetorical question. In modern Japanese it is mainly used as a sentence-final question particle.
formation: The core of 「か」 is “uncertainty”. At the end of a sentence it marks the whole sentence as something the speaker is unsure about and wants answered, so it becomes a question (after 「です」「ます」, a polite one). Between nouns or verbs (「AかB」, 「行くか行かないか」) it means “it is unclear which of the two”, i.e. a choice. When a question containing a question word is placed inside a larger sentence, it no longer asks anything of the listener but becomes the object of verbs like 「分かる」 or 「教える」: an embedded question. And when you pose a question whose answer is obviously “no” (「誰が信じるか」), the question turns into a rhetorical one that strongly denies. All these uses grow out of the single idea of uncertainty.

similar.title: 〜question word + か (indefinite)
similar.explanation: The same 「か」 (same origin): in 「何か」 and 「誰か」, 「か」 means “some~” and isn't asking anything: 「何か食べますか」 means “Would you like something to eat?”.

similar.title: 〜と〜とどちらが
similar.explanation: Both are used to choose one of two and are close in meaning: 「AかB」 just gives the options; 「AとBとどちらが〜」 asks the listener to compare and choose: 「コーヒーと紅茶とどちらがいいですか」.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: Both are sentence-ending particles and are often compared: 「〜ですか」 is a real question when you don't know the answer; 「〜ですね」 checks or seeks agreement when the speaker already has the answer in mind.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Both put several things together and are easily confused: 「AやB」 lists examples and can include all of them; 「AかB」 picks only one.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜ものか」is dedicated to strong denial and resolve, so its meaning is clear. A bare 「〜か」is rougher and blunter and depends more on intonation.

meaning: Placed at the end of a sentence to seek agreement, or to confirm something both speakers know. It sounds friendly and soft, a bit like English “..., isn't it?” or “..., right?”.
connection: Sentence (plain form／です・ます form) + ね

senses.label: Seeking agreement
senses.meaning: The speaker assumes the listener feels the same and uses 「ね」 to invite agreement: “isn't it?”, “don't you think?”. Common when commenting on the weather, food and so on.
senses.connection: Adjective／noun + です + ね; い-adjective + ね
examples: Nice weather today, isn't it?
This cake is delicious, isn't it?
Your Japanese is really good.

senses.label: Confirming
senses.meaning: Checks whether something you know or guess is correct: “..., right?”. The tone rises slightly.
senses.connection: Sentence + ね (↗); 〜ですよね
examples: Tomorrow's meeting starts at ten, right?
You're Mr. Tanaka, aren't you?
This is your umbrella, right?

senses.label: Softening / gentle reminders
senses.meaning: At the end of reminders, promises or goodbyes, it makes the tone warm and soft.
senses.connection: 〜てね／〜ましょうね／じゃあ、また〜ね
examples: Get home safely, OK?
See you tomorrow, then.

notes: To tell someone new information they don't know, use 「よ」, not 「ね」: to say “Tomorrow's a day off, just so you know”, say 「明日は休みですよ」. 「明日は休みですね」 turns it into a check: “Tomorrow's a day off, right?”
Saying 「上手ですね」 or 「よくできましたね」 to a superior or someone older evaluates their ability. It sounds condescending and is quite rude; you can say 「勉強になりました」 instead.
Requests ending in 「ね」 like 「待っててね」 or 「お願いね」 are too casual for clients or superiors. Say 「お待ちください」 or 「よろしくお願いします」.
Adding 「ね」 to every sentence sounds childish or clingy. Use it in moderation in formal situations.

etymology: 「ね」 is a sentence-final particle that spread in spoken Japanese from the Edo period on. It brings the speaker closer to the listener. One theory links it to the old particle 「な」, used for emotion and gentle urging.

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: Both are sentence-ending particles and are the pair most often compared: 「ね」 is for information both people share, seeking agreement or confirmation; 「よ」 is for information the listener doesn't know, with a tone of reminding or asserting. Together, 「よね」 means “That's what I think, and you think so too, right?”

similar.title: 〜なあ・〜な (exclamation)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express emotion, and some say they're related in origin. 「なあ」 is mostly an exclamation to yourself (「いいなあ」); 「ね」 is directed at the listener to share a feeling or confirm (「いいですね」).

similar.title: 〜でしょう (guess / confirmation)
similar.explanation: Both can be used to confirm and are close in meaning: 「〜でしょう？」 sounds more certain than 「ね」 and can come across as pushy toward a superior.

formation: 「ね」 is a single sentence-ending particle. It “hands the remark over to the listener”, inviting them to agree. So it can only be used for things the speaker assumes the listener also knows or will agree with: seeking agreement (「いい天気ですね」) or confirming (「明日ですね」). After a request, it turns the demand into “we're agreed, right?”, which softens the tone. Stretched to 「ねえ」, the “handing over” function gets stronger, so at the start of a sentence it becomes a way of calling for attention: “Hey”.
